questions.title_en: Falsifying prophecy that is YET to be fulfilled
questions.question:
In the Torah, the definition of a false prophet relies on his prediction not to be fulfilled (Deut 19.1):

וְכִי תֹאמַר בִּלְבָבֶךָ אֵיכָה נֵדַע אֶת־הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר לֹא־דִבְּרוֹ יְהֹוָה׃
אֲשֶׁר יְדַבֵּר הַנָּבִיא בְּשֵׁם יְהֹוָה וְלֹא־יִהְיֶה הַדָּבָר וְלֹא יָבֹא
הוּא הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר לֹא־דִבְּרוֹ יְהֹוָה בְּזָדוֹן דִּבְּרוֹ הַנָּבִיא לֹא תָגוּר מִמֶּנּוּ׃
And should you ask yourselves, “How can we know that the oracle was not spoken by God?”— if the prophet speaks in the name of God and the oracle does not come true, that oracle was not spoken by God;"

We clearly see that many biblical prophecies are interpreted by our sages as "to be fulfilled" in the future, at the end of days, for example, the Messiah or the return of a Davidic monarch, even when the scriptural timespan passed.

How can a false prophecy be falsified if the prophet can always claim "It is YET to be fulfilled"?

questions.title_en: Why in Deuteronomy does Moses introduce 200 new Mitzvot?
questions.question:
The Book of Numbers concludes the Torah narrative from the creation, through the Exodus, the Receiving of the Torah, the 40 years of the wilderness to make the Exodus generation go extinct, up to the moment of entering the promised land. It ends with the following verse:

"אֵלֶּה הַמִּצְוֺת וְהַמִּשְׁפָּטִים אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהֹוָה בְּיַד־מֹשֶׁה אֶל־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּעַרְבֹת מוֹאָב עַל יַרְדֵּן יְרֵחוֹ׃"
"These are the commandments and laws that God commanded upon the Israelites, through Moses, on the steppes of Moab, at the Jordan near Jericho."

In the following book, Deuteronomy, Moses orients the new generation of settlers by providing a long recap of the period in the wilderness. In his speech, in addition to stories and complaints, he introduces 200 (!) additional Mitzvos, despite the aforementioned ending verse in Numbers.

I can't wrap my mind around this fact:

  • If those Mitzvos were already known to all, why weren't they all included in the previous books, for example, the multiple Mitzvos learned from שמע ישראל?
  • If they were not known and heard for the first time, why aren't they prefaced with "וידבר ה' למשה לאמר" or something similar to reflect their divinity and not Moses' addition? Alternatively, can we say that the Torah has changed to reflect the characteristics of the new generation, for example, the Mitzva to love God with all your heart?
  • If they were known only to Moses, why didn't he relay them to his generation? Didn't they put Teffilin or recite Shemah?

answers.text:
I will use R. Chaim Jachter's comments on Sefer Devarim with added sources.

Moshe Rabbeinu delivered the speeches in Sefer Devarim, who wrote the speeches? Using example of the curses in parashas Ki Savo, Megilla 31b implies that Moshe Rabbeinu composed Sefer Devarim. For example, Rashi clarifies:

Moshe spoke [the words] from the Mouth of the Might and was made into a messanger "Holy One Blessed be He said to me so", therefore [in Parashas Bechukosai it says]: "I will place, I will make you pay, I will send" - the One who is capable to do so. However, in the Mishneh Torah it is written "Hashem will hit, Hashem will attach to you". Moshe said [these words] on his own if the [Jewish people] transgress the commandments, Hashem will make them pay for it.

Tosafot (ad. loc.) clarify that Moshe Rabbeinu wrote it with Ru’ach HaKodesh, divine inspiration. This means that Hashem influenced Moshe Rabbeinu in his composition of the speeches. However, Tosafot does not state that Moshe Rabbeinu wrote Devarim with Nevu’ah, prophecy. Moshe Rabbeinu did have input into the speech. While it is difficult, if not impossible, to know where Hashem’s influence ended and Moshe Rabbeinu’s autonomy began, the Gemara clearly states that Moshe Rabbeinu had at least a measure of independence in the composition of the speeches recorded in Sefer Devarim.

Moreover, Moshe Rabbeinu certainly did not devise the Mitzvot that appear for the first time in Sefer Devarim. Instead, what Moshe Rabbeinu is doing is presenting Mitzvot which he heard from Hashem at Har Sinai but until now were simply Torah SheBe’al Peh as noted in Shemot 34:32 with Chizkuni:

all the commandments that G-d had spoken to him about while he had been on Mount Sinai on his first and third stay on the Mountain, as well as all the commandments that He had communicated to him from Nissan when they had left Egypt until the twentieth of Iyar in the second year when they broke camp around the Mountain. However, according to the Talmud in tractate Gittin folio 60, the written Torah, i.e. in scroll form, he wrote down personally, one parchment at a time. When Moses made ready to leave this earth, he arranged these parchments in the order in which we read them nowadays according to the order he considered appropriate.

Also the introductions of the Ramban to Sefer Devarim:

Additionally, he (Moshe) proclaims commandments which have not been [previously] mentioned at all, such as the levirate marriage, the law concerning the defamation of a virgin bride, the divorcing of a wife, [the punishment of] plotting witnesses, and others besides. Now all these laws had in fact been declared to Moses, either on Sinai or in the Tent of Meeting within the first year [of the erection of the Tabernacle] before the affair of the spies. Nothing new was revealed to Moses in the plains of Moab [where he held this review of the Torah] except the words of the covenant, as is expressly stated there. It is for this reason that this book does not contain such statements as “And G-d spoke to Moses, saying:Command the children of Israel,” or “Speak to the children of Israel and say to them the following commandment” [since no new commandments were given in this book; they had all been previously declared to Moses either on Mount Sinai or in the Tent of Meeting]. These commandments, however, were not written in the preceding books wherein He speaks to those that came forth from Egypt. Perhaps this was because these commandments were obligatory only in the Land even though they affect personal conduct [and do not depend on the Land] such as Scripture mentions with reference to the drink-offerings; or it may be that because these were not of common occurrence, he mentioned them only to the generation, the inheritors of the Land.

For example, R. Jachter notes that in Sefer Shemot (20:14), Hashem commands us not to be jealous of our neighbor’s wife, his ox and donkey, and all that belongs to his neighbor. However, in Sefer Devarim Moshe Rabbeinu formulates (according to the Pashtanim such as Ibn Ezra) the prohibition as forbidding jealousy of one’s neighbor’s wife, house, field, ox, and anything he has. in the Midbar we did not have homes and we did not have fields. Now that we in Sefer Devarim are about to enter Eretz Yisrael the concern for jealousy of one’s neighbor’s house and field becomes very relevant.

The subject is discussed by Abarbanel to in his introduction to Sefer Devarim. Abarbanel clarifies that Hashem is the author of Sefer Devarim since Hashem is quoting Moshe Rabbeinu with His approval and even possibly edits his speeches for inclusion in the Torah (as for example, discussed here). Abarbanel fits beautifully with Chagigah 15b that teaches that Hashem cites the original Torah thoughts of the great Chachamim. While Hashem undoubtedly influences the Chachamim (see Mishna, Yadayim 4:3), they also have some degree of autonomy. Hashem cites the great Chachamim with approval just as He approvingly presents Moshe Rabbeinu’s speeches in Sefer Devarim.

questions.title_en: Is the term "Memra" (Word) in the Targum Jerusalem Deuteronomy 24:7 connected with Avot De Rabbi Natan 34:9 and Sefer Yetzirah 1:9?
questions.question:
Targum Jerusalem Deuteronomy 26:17 goes like this:

"You have chosen the Word of the Lord to be king over You this day, that he may be your God."

Does this unique concept called "Word" have something to do with Avot De Rabbi Natan 34:9:

"The Holy Spirit is referred to by ten terms. And they are: Parable, Metaphor, Riddle, Speech, Saying, Splendor, Command, Burden, Prophecy, Vision."

Or Sefer Yetzirah 1:9:

"Ten Sefirot-Without-What: One – Spirit of the Living God, blessed and glorified is the name of the life of the worlds, voice and spirit and speech. This is the Holy Spirit."?

And could it be that its origin can be traced from works of Philo Judeaus, Midrash Tanchuma Bo 5:3, Midrash Tanchuma Buber Yitro 17:1, and the Divine Voice in Apocalypse of Abraham?

answers.text:
Based on the extracts copied and pasted below, my answer is that I can see no link at all between Targum Jerusalem Deuteronomy 26:17, Avot De Rabbi Natan 34:9 and Sefer Yetzirah 1:9

Sefaria at https://www.sefaria.org/Targum_Jerusalem%2C_Deuteronomy.26.15-17?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en has the Aramaic original text of the Targum Deuteronomy 26:17 as:

יַת מֵימְרָא דַיְיָ אַמְלִיכְתּוּן עֲלֵיכוֹן יוֹמָא דֵין לְמֶהֱוֵי לְכוֹן לֶאֱלָהָא:

With the English as follows:

You have chosen the Word of the Lord to be King over you this day, that He may be your God.

Sefaria at https://www.sefaria.org/Avot_DeRabbi_Natan.34.8-9?lang=bi has the original text and translation of Avot d’Rabbi Natan 34:9 as follows:

עשרה שמות נקרא רוח הקדש. אלו הן משל. מליצה. חידה. דיבור. אמירה. תפארת. ציווי. משא. נבואה. חזיון: The Holy Spirit is referred to by ten terms. And they are: Parable, Metaphor, Riddle, Speech, Saying, Splendor, Command, Burden, Prophecy, Vision.

Sefaria at https://www.sefaria.org/Sefer_Yetzirah.1.8-9?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en Has Sefer Yetzirah in the original and in English as follows:

עשר ספירות בלימה, אחת רוח אלהים חיים ברוך ומבורך שמו של חי העולמים קול ורוח ודבור וזהו רוח הקדש: Ten Sefirot-Without-What: One – Spirit of the Living God, blessed and glorified is the name of the life of the worlds, voice and spirit and speech. This is the Holy Spirit.

questions.title_en: The written Torah
questions.question: Moses brought the Ten Commandments down from Mount Sinai but our modern Torah contains more than just that. So when was the Torah as we have it today written?

answers.text:
We see from many places that the rest of the Torah was also given at Sinai, and/or in the desert. See for instance https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus.27.34?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en

אֵ֣לֶּה הַמִּצְוֺ֗ת אֲשֶׁ֨ר צִוָּ֧ה ה' אֶת־מֹשֶׁ֖ה אֶל־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל בְּהַ֖ר סִינָֽי׃
These are the commandments that Hashem gave Moses for the Israelite people on Mount Sinai.

You can also see in many places that Moses was teaching the Torah to Israel as they went through the time of Sinai and the desert. As to when it was written down, that is more subtle. There are two opinions given in the gemara in Gittin 60a: Was it written down as it was taught (מגילה מגילה ניתנה) or written down all at once at the end (חתומה ניתנה).

questions.title_en: Is there any explanation on whether Terach knew that Nimrod would kill the slave baby that he substituted for Avrohom
questions.question: It seems that Nimrod changed drastically over time to become so narcissitic and murderous. I am not clear where Terach sits in the middle of that politically - Is there any explanation or discussions on the close relationship between Terach and Nimrod?Historical story R. Nissin Mindel Z'l How was Terach viewed on the balance as a rasha or a tzadik? Did Terach know that Nimrod would violently murder the slave child Terach exchanged for Avrohom his son (subterfuge) or was Nimrod's wicked response a surprise to Terach - perhaps in those days that type of thing was accepted/common in that era? (Horrific but possible?!?) And was there any other option that Terach could have had in that scenario?

answers.text:
It states in Rashi Bereshit 11:32 about Terach:

Therefore, Scripture calls him dead, for the wicked, even in their lifetime, are called dead

However it also states in Rashi Bereshit 15:15

His father was an idolater, and He announces to him that he will come to him? This teaches you that Terah repented. [from Tan. Shemoth 18]

So he was seen as wicked - in fact Avraham breaks from his philosophy etc...; however, he does repent and become righteous at some point after Avraham leaving and before his own death.

questions.title_en: Torah service on shabbat with no kohanim and not enough yisraelim
questions.question:
If there are no kohanim in shul on shabbat, Ashkenazi practice is to give the first aliyah to a levi or yisrael, and the subsequent six aliyot to yisraelim. (See Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim 135:6,9,10.)

What happens if there are no kohanim and five or fewer yisraelim, with the rest of the minyan made up of leviim? Presumably in these cases, one would give aliyot to more than one levi.

How should the seven aliyot be distributed between the leviim and yisraelim?

Ideally, answers should address the six cases ranging from zero yisraelim to five yisraelim, and specify which aliyot go to which type of person in each case.

(I’m asking mainly about these specific scenarios in order to keep the question more manageable. Feel free to expand your answer to include other scenarios with one or more kohanim, some leviim and insufficient yisraelim.)

answers.text:
The regular rules for Aliyah positions are based on three rules: 1) kohen and levi read first if available to avoid fighting about who reads first (Gittin 59a), 2) a kohen should not read directly after a different kohen, nor levi after another levi, so as not to make people wonder if the first one was found to be invalid (Gittin 59b), 3) some say Rule 2 applies even if the two are not directly adjacent since the latter 5 aliyot are generally for Yisraelim some might come to question the validity of the latter kohen/levi (cf. Shulchan Aruch OC 135:10), and some say not to worry about this third rule if calling another Kohen-Levi-Yisrael triad (cf. Mishna Berura, ibid :37).

The Shulchan Aruch (OC 135:12) rules that if you're stuck then we allow breaking all those rules. Since Rule 3 is highly disputed, that'd be the first to go. Accordingly, it comes out that you basically do as close to a repeating Kohen-Levi-Yisrael as possible as many times as needed to fill out 7 people.

There are two caveats to keep in mind. First, if the case is one with at least one Yisrael and no Levi, then the first triplet would be Kohen-Kohen-Yisrael like an ordinary situation of no Levi, but not subsequent triplets since those are arguably not actually necessary as triplets. Second, if there are only Kohanim and exactly one other, or only Leviyim and exactly one Yisrael, the Shulchan Aruch (:12) rules we flip the script and put the singleton first to avoid fighting and continue with repeating statuses from there.

Example case of 2 Leviyim and 1 Yisrael: Kohen, Levi, Yisrael, Kohen, Levi, Kohen, Kohen.

Example case of 0 Leviyim and 3 Yisraelim: Kohen, same Kohen, Yisrael, Kohen, Yisrael, Kohen, Yisrael.

Example case of 0 Leviyim and 1 Yisrael: Yisrael, Kohen, Kohen, Kohen, Kohen, Kohen, Kohen.

questions.title_en: Maase Miriam on the way of leaving Egypt?
questions.question:
The Torah in this week's Parsha tells us on Deut.24:9 to remember what Hashem did to Miriam on the way of getting out of Egypt.

I looked at the most commentaries from the Rishonim and could not find an answer to the following question: why does the Torah stresses out "on the way of getting out of Egypt"? Seemingly this verse is referring to what happened to Miriam, end of Parshat Behaalotcha, nearly one year after camping at the foot of Mount Sinai. Is that still considered Egypt?

answers.text:
The answer is given in Midrash Sifrei Devarim 275:2-3:

בדרך, בשעת טירופכם

on the way: when you were tossed about.

בצאתכם ממצרים, בשעת גאולתכם אלא שתלה הכתוב במרים ללמדך שכל זמן שהיו הדגלים נוסעים לא היו הולכים עד שמרים מקדמת לפניהם וכן הוא אומר (מיכה ו ד) ואשלח לפניך את משה אהרן ומרים סליק פיסקא

when you left Egypt: the time of your redemption, and all was stopped because of her, whereby we are apprised that all of that time when the standards of the tribes traveled, they did so only when Miriam preceded them, viz. (Michah 6:4) "In fact, I brought you up from the land of Egypt, I redeemed you from the house of bondage, And I sent before you Moses, Aaron, and Miriam."

In other words, the time of geula, based on the verse in Micha, is called "getting out of Mitzraim" (physically and spiritually), and it was marked by Moshe, Aharon, and Miriam leading Jewish people. However, because of Miriam's punishment, the whole travel was halted and everyone had to wait for her.

questions.title_en: Word switching from plural to singular when it is many?
questions.question:
In Shir HaShirim (5:11), Rashi writes: "רְבָבוֹת הַרְבֵּה קְרוּיִין רְבָבָה, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "רְבָבָה כְּצֶמַח הַשָׂדֶה נְתַתִּיךְ": Many myriads are called ‘רְבָבָה’, as it is stated, “Myriads רְבָבָה like the vegetation of the field have I made you.”

So the plural word רְבָבוֹת becomes singular (רְבָבָה) when there are many of it. Are there any other examples in Lashon HaKodesh of a word switching from plural to singular when there are many of it?

answers.text:
It seems that the plural is dropped when the number of objects is large enough that the individuals are indistinguishable within the mass, in which case they are simply referred to as a single mass of x species. In the same way that Rashi (Bereishis 1:11) explains דשא as “vegetation” as a concept as opposed to individual “plants”, a hoard of men will be described as “man” (e.g. Shoftim 7:23 ויצעק איש ישראל - “the Israelite man rallied”.) In this case, “man” is merely identifying the species of which the mass is comprised.

Some more examples: ומלאו את הארץ חלל - “they filled the earth with ‘corpse’” (Yechezkel 30:11)

ולא ימיש מעשות פֶרי - “it does not cease to give fruit” (Yirmiyah 17:8)

וסוס ורכב רב מאד - “and horse and chariot, a great many” (Yehoshua 11:4)

The more difficult it is to distinguish the individual, the more natural this becomes. We would not expect the word חול - “sand” to have a plural form, because we are referring to the abstract mass, not just to a large group of sand grains.

This happens pretty frequently with nouns in Hebrew, when either a large unspecified number is meant, or a number larger than ten.

See eg Bereishit 32:6 or Shemot 26:19.

questions.title_en: Should one pay more than one fifth (20%) for goods or services from a fellow Jew?
questions.question:
On a recent shiur, a Rov mentioned that one is supposed to spend up to a fifth (20%) more on goods or services provided by a fellow Jew. So for example, if you're in a Jewish bookstore and they're selling a book that's a couple dollars cheaper on Amazon, it would be preferable to purchase it from the Jewish bookstore, even for more than it's listed on Amazon, as long as it's not over 20% more expensive.

Is there a source for this minhag? Is it a halacha?

This was specifically referring to a non-mitzva related item. Just general business transactions.

answers.text: Rav Moshe Zvi Neria wrote that one must buy produce from Jews, even if it costs up to a third more. His teacher Rav Kook concurred but rejected the one-third limit, saying there is no limit. [Likutei HaRe’iyah, Kfar Haroeh, 1991, pp. 279-280.] The Rema said one must support Jewish businesses even if their price is higher.[Teshuvot HaRema 10] However, the Chafetz Chayyim ruled that there is no obligation, but it is preferable to deal with Jewish businesses, even if the cost is slightly higher. [Ahavat Chesed 5:6-7] I think the halacha of the matter is not completely settled.

questions.title_en: Does Deut. 34:10 mean that Joshua wasn’t the prophet like Moses?
questions.question:
I used to think Deuteronomy 18:18

I will raise them up a prophet from among their brethren, like you, and will put My words in his mouth

was about Jesus but I see the Jews believe it’s about Joshua which makes a lot of sense after reading Joshua 1.

However, my confusion comes in when Deuteronomy 34:10

And there arose not a prophet since in Yisra᾽el like Moshe, whom the Lord knew face to face

is read because it seems to indicate that the prophet like Moses has to speak directly to יהוה like Moses did.

Does Deut. 34:10 mean that Joshua wasn’t the prophet like Moses? If not Joshua, who is the prophet described in Deut. 18:18?

answers.text:
The prophet who immediately succeeded Moses as leader was Joshua, and this bestowal of leadership begins in Numbers 27:15-23. As you mentioned, we indeed see the Almighty speak prophetically to Joshua in Joshua 1:1-9, and He was with Joshua as He was with Moses (3:7).

Nonetheless, the context of Deuteronomy 18 indicates that it is not only about Joshua, but about a series of true prophets who would continue to guide the Children of Israel throughout many future generations. As such, the singular word "נביא" (prophet) is referring to a template for a class of true prophets. Likewise, 18:19-22 speaks in a parallel manner of a template of false prophets who must be rejected, and the singular "נביא" is used even though such false prophets arose in multiple later generations (see, e.g., I Kings 22 and Jeremiah 28:10-17).

As you mentioned, Moses had a sui generis type of prophecy ("face to face") that would never be achieved by anyone else (Deut. 34:10-12). Various commentators have addressed the meaning of "like you" in Deut. 18:15,18, and some of them point out explicitly that the similarity of this prophet to Moses does not extend to the advanced level of prophecy that Moses achieved.1

Targum Yerushalmi (Deut. 18:15, "דְּדָמֵי לִי בְּרוּחַ קוּדְשָׁא") explains the similarity to be that the future prophets will be infused with a prophetic spirit of holiness.

Rashi (ad loc., "כמו שאני מקרבך מאחיך יקים לך תחתי וכן מנביא לנביא") explains the point of similarity to be that future prophets will be like Moses insofar as they will emerge from the brethren within the Children of Israel. Thus, Rashi reads the verse as, "A prophet who will be from your midst, from your brethren, [and as such will be] like me."

Rashbam (ad loc.) explains that the prophet will be like Moses in exhorting the Children of Israel to follow the Torah, unlike a false prophet or dreamer who tells Israel to worship idolatry. The Rashbam adds that Deut. 34:10 should be interpreted to read, "And no other prophet arose in Israel like Moses, [insofar as] he knew the Lord face to face," while prophets would arise who would be similar to Moses in other respects.

Ibn Ezra (ad loc., "כמוני שהוא נביא השם לא מנחש") provides a similar explanation that future true prophets would be prophets of the Almighty, and not sorcerous diviners.

The Ramban (ad loc., "וכן על דעתי 'כמוני' שיהיה נאמן לנביא לה' ותאמין בו כאשר אתה מאמין בי") provides a similar explanation, that the true prophets would be similar to Moses insofar as being a faithful prophet of the Almighty, and that the Children of Israel should trust in such a prophet just as they trusted in Moses.

Rabbeinu Bechaye (ad loc.) explains that the prophet described in Deut. 18:15,18 is Joshua, but can also include the series of later prophets who would guide Israel. Rabbeinu Bechaye provides an explanation of "like me" which is similar to Rashi's explanation, and Rabbeinu Bechaye explains that the repeated language is necessary to drive home the point that future prophets for Israel would not merely emerge from distant "brethren" (namely the descendants of Esau or Ishmael), but only from the Children of Israel themselves.

Rabbeinu Bechaye also provides another explanation similar to the Rashbam, that future true prophets would never seek to permanently or completely uproot any of the commandments of the Torah, and at most they would have the authority to temporarily suspend observance of a commandment in some cases for certain exigencies (see Y'vamos 90b).

Finally, Rabbeinu Bechaye points out that the Children of Israel believed Moses not because of the miracles Moses performed, but rather because the entire congregation of Israel heard the Almighty's voice together with Moses and therefore knew that later pronouncements they would hear from Moses were from a true and reliable prophet. In a similar vein, the Children of Israel would establish future prophets not on the basis of miracles, but on the basis of verifying their prophecy and thereby establishing them as authentic prophets going forward (see Deut. 18:21-22).

1 The New Testament passage to which you alluded (Acts 3:19-23) is a christological eisegesis that injects Christian interpretation into verses in the Hebrew Bible by ignoring the context of Deut. 18.

questions.title_en: Did the Jews do anything to merit the end of the Persian exile?
questions.question: Whereas during the slavery in Egyptian the Torah indicates that the Jews cried out and their cries reached Hashem, I am not aware of any similar verse which indicates the Jews did any action which led to the end of their exile under Darius. I realize that the exile had to come to an end at some point because it was prophesized to last for 70 years, however I would like to know if the sages propose any action on the part of the people which triggered the end of their exile at that time.

answers.text:
R. Michoel Miller, a scholar of Maharal, wrote a small book "Darkness and Destiny: The Four Empires in Midrash and Beyond" which collects all midrashic and outside sources on the four kingdoms. Unfortunately, it does not have a commentary, but it did pointed out for me the Midrash Bereshis Rabba 99:2 which gives cryptic reasons for the fall of each of the four empires.

Here's the part relevant to the question asked:

Benjamin opposite the kingdom of Media – this one was likened to a wolf, and that one was likened to a wolf. This one was likened to a wolf: “Benjamin is a wolf that mauls” (Genesis 49:27); and that one was likened to a wolf: “Behold another, a second beast, resembling a bear [ledov]” (Daniel 7:5) – Rabbi Ḥanina said: Ledov is written, but it was called dev. (Commentary: *The word dov, bear, is sometimes written with a vav. In this instance it is written without a vav, such that it can be read dev, which is Aramaic for ze’ev, wolf. Thus, the midrash is saying that Media is compared to a wolf.) This is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yoḥanan, as Rabbi Yoḥanan said: ... “a wolf of the deserts will plunder them” (Jeremiah 5:6) – this is Media. Into the hands of whom did the kingdom of Media fall? Into the hands of Mordekhai, who descended from Benjamin.

The midrash is amaizingly cryptic, so what does it mean? First of all, according to wikipedia, wolves live in packs which are led by strong leaders. Therefore, the midrash notes that in Persia there was a problem of the community leadership and internal community strife.

We know, that Persian empire offered people unbelievable freedom, so that any girl could become a queen. Yalkut Meam Loez 1:5 in the name of Yearos D'vash points that the seven day banquet in Shushan began during the 10 days of repentance on the 3rd of Tishrei and ended on Yom Kippur (with kosher food). That was why Mordekhai protested that people should not come to the banquet, but they did not listen.

Rabbeinu Bachya ibn Pekudah in his commentary on Shemos 38:25 points another problem among the Jews: they no longer viewed each other as equal members one community. Why did Haman offer 10,000 kikar of silver to Achashveirosh to eliminate all the jews, which weighted against the 100 kikar of shekalim brought by 600,000 Jews? Haman used the bigest valuation of Arachin, 50 shekels (Vayikra 27:3) per male. Compared to half-shekel, 50 shekalim gives a factor of 100 and 10,000 = 100*100. In other words, Haman's accusation against the Jews was that even when raising money we did it according to the laws of Arachin (individually) and not according to the laws of Shekalim (same value for everyone).

Certainly, the point of Rabbeinu Bachya also goes against the rule that in a pack of wolves everyone but the leader is equal. Today we fix these problems with the mitzvah of shekalim before Purim and sending the same mishloach manos, and of course with recognising the true value of Torah leaders like Mordekhai. Additional important point is made in gemara Shabbos 88a:

Rava said: Even so, they again accepted it willingly in the time of Ahasuerus, as it is written: “The Jews ordained, and took upon them, and upon their seed, and upon all such as joined themselves unto them” (Esther 9:27), and he taught: The Jews ordained what they had already taken upon themselves through coercion at Sinai.

Finally, the above midrash Bereshis Rabba 99:2 fits well with historical calculations in the book by R. Alexander Hool "The Challenge of Jewish History", which shows that Achashverosh was Cambyses and the son of Esther Darius the 1st had lost the war to Alexander the Great (contrary to the academic historical dogma from Herodotus that it was Darius the 3rd). See also, Carl Olof Jonsson "The Gentile Times Reconsidered".

questions.title_en: Ki Savo: Idols of Wood and Stone
questions.question:
Devarim 28:64 says:

וֶהֱפִֽיצְךָ֤ יְהֹוָה֙ בְּכׇל־הָ֣עַמִּ֔ים מִקְצֵ֥ה הָאָ֖רֶץ וְעַד־קְצֵ֣ה הָאָ֑רֶץ וְעָבַ֨דְתָּ שָּׁ֜ם אֱלֹהִ֣ים אֲחֵרִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֧ר לֹא־יָדַ֛עְתָּ אַתָּ֥ה וַאֲבֹתֶ֖יךָ עֵ֥ץ וָאָֽבֶן׃

יהוה will scatter you among all the peoples from one end of the earth to the other, and there you shall serve other gods, wood and stone, whom neither you nor your ancestors have experienced

Of course, the galus part came true literally, but I am wondering about the אֱלֹהִ֣ים אֲחֵרִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֧ר לֹא־יָדַ֛עְתָּ אַתָּ֥ה וַאֲבֹתֶ֖יךָ עֵ֥ץ וָאָֽבֶן.

B’zmanenu, there are still certain groups who perform avodah zara for wooden idols, but they are not at all dominant outside of India l’choira.

Rashi writes:

ועבדתם שם אלהים אחרים. כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ — לֹא עֲבוֹדַת אֱלֹהוּת מַמָּשׁ אֶלָּא מַעֲלִים מַס וְגֻלְגֹּלִיּוֹת לְכוּמְרֵי עֲ"זָ: ועבדתם שם אלהים אחרים

AND YE WILL SERVE THERE OTHER GODS — Understand this as the Targum does: (ye will serve the peoples that worship idols); not actually that they shall serve idols, but they will have to pay tribute and poll-taxes to the priests of the idols.

This makes sense in Rashi’s France, when his government was explicitly Christian, but how do we understand this for our generation?

Are our “idols” money and values contrary to Torah? Are the “priests” politicians and bureaucrats?

Edit: this question is distinct from another question regarding the idea of contemporary nochri idolatry in that it is with reference to this particular pasuk.

answers.text:
The Satmar Rav (Divrei Yoel Al HaMoadim, Shekalim, Zachor, Purim, p. 54-55 ff.) explains that nowadays, we have different kind of avodah zarah than there was back in the days. He says:

כי הנה כן אנו רואים היום שמלבישים תמיד איזה צורה אחרת לעבודה זרה ועל ידי זה כבר נמשכים אחריה שאומרים שאינו כמו אותו עד עכשיו אלא שהוא באופן אחר

For indeed, we see today that idolatry is constantly being disguised in new forms, and through this disguise, people are led astray after it. They claim that it is not the same as the idolatry of the past but something different

וזאת ועוד נוסף כי אכן לאמיתו של דבר הרי המתבונן מבחין שבאמת נשאר הכל ממש כאותו העבודה זרה שהיתה מלפנים אלא שיש בכוחו של היצר הרע לטכס עצה ולמצוא תמיד איזה לבוש שונה באופן אחר שיוכל להלביש בזה את העבודה זרה שתהיה נראית שהיא אחרת

Moreover, upon closer reflection, one can discern that in reality, nothing has changed—it remains exactly the same idolatry as it was before. The only difference is that the evil inclination has the ability to devise new strategies and continuously find different ways to cloak idolatry in various forms

So, according to the opinion of the Satmar Rav, avodah zarah changes. De avodah zarah of the time of pharao is not the same as we have now, but the foundational ideas are the same.

He says:

ומעתה נאמר שכל זה רמוז באומרו לא יהיה לך אלהים אחרים דהנה אמרו ז"ל במכילתא מכילתא ס' בחודש פ"ס ומובא ברש"י שמוח כ' ג' לבאר אומרו לא יהיה וגו' על פני כל זמן שאני קיים שלא תאמר שלא נצטוו על ע"ז אלא אותו הדור ע"כ ולדרכינו הכוונה שלא תאמר שלא נצטוו אלא על אותו הלבוש והדמות שהיתה נראית העבודה זרה שבאותו הדור ולכן אמר אלהים אחרים היינו שנצטוו גם אפילו אם ישתנו דמותי וצורות הע"ז שיהיו נראין באופן אחר מכפי שהיו אז וכדבר האמור שהצורות והלבושים שלהם משתנים תמיד וזהו כוונת אומרו שאלו נפרש להם כל שם ע"ז לא היה מספיק כל העורות שבעולם דהנה גם אצל פרעה לא היו רק אותם הע"ז שהיו אז בימיו אבל לא היה יודע מה שיהיה אחריו וכל אופני שמות העבודה זרה שיש בימינו אלה לא היה לו בספרו אמנם כוונת המכילתא הוא על כל אופני העבודה זרה שיתחדשו בהמשך כל הדורות ועל כך אמרו שאכן אם ירצו לכתוב כולם מה שהיו בהמשך הזמנים ועד לימינו אלה בעיקבתא דמשיחא שתמיד משתנים בדמותם ולבושיהם השונים הרי ודאי שלא היה מספיק כל העורות שבעולם כי אין להם שיעור

As we mentioned earlier, the forms and appearances of idolatry are constantly changing. This is what the verse means when it says that if we were to specify the name of every idol, all the hides in the world would not suffice. Just as in the time of Pharaoh, only the idols of his time were known, but he had no knowledge of the idols that would come after him, nor did his book contain the names of all the forms of idolatry that exist in our time. The intention of the Mechilta is to encompass all forms of idolatry that will arise throughout the generations. And they said that if one were to attempt to write down all the forms of idolatry that have existed from then until today, in the footsteps of the Messiah, where idolatry constantly changes its form and appearance, all the hides in the world would not suffice, for there is no limit to them

One can use the quoted passage to include atheism. In colleges professors like to tell a story that polytheists worship many gods, monotheists worship one god, and then there are progressive atheists who do not worship anyone. As an answer, one can use the comment of R. Eliyahu Mizrachi on Rashi Bereshis 18:4, which defines atheism as avoda zara:

ורחצו רגליכם כסבור שהם ערביים כו'. במציעא פרק השוכר את הפועלים ולאו מרחיצה קא מפיק לה דאם כן לבן שלא היה מקפיד למה נתן להם מים לרחוץ וכן לוט שלא היה מקפיד שהרי הקדי' לינה לרחיצה למה נתן להם לרחוץ אלא עכ"ל דרחיצה אורחא דמילתא היא לכל הולכי דרכים והא דדרז"ל אינו אלא מדהקדים רחיצה לביאה שלא כדרך המנהג שמנהג העולם להכניסם תחלה ואחר כך לרחוץ והיינו דמסיים אבל לוט שלא הקפיד הקדים לינה לרחיצה כלומר כפי דרך המנהג לא כאברהם דאם לא כן מה טעם להזכיר כאן את לוט ונראה לי דאבק רגליהם לאו דוקא אלא לכל אבק הם משתחוים והא דנקט אבק רגליהם משום דאורחייהו דהולכי דרכים להמצא האבק ברגליהם והא דלא הקפיד בהם על שהיו עובדי כוכבים להכניסם בביתו הוא משו' דאין מקפידין על העובדי' אלא על הנעבדי' שהם עבודת כוכבים עצמם ומפני שכל הלומדים תמהי' על זה היאך אפשר להיות שישתחוה שום אדם לאבק שעל רגליו שהוא הפחות שבנמצאות נראה לי לתת טעם על זה שמפני שהקדמוני' מהפלוסופים היו מאמינים שכל הנמצאות כלם מורכבים מהעצמים הפרדיים שהם האבק ושבחבורם יתהוו כל הנמצאים ובהפרדם יפסדו ושאין מנהיג זולתם רק הם עצמם האלוהו' כמו כת אפיקורוס וסיעתו והאבק נמצא תמיד ברגלי הולכי דרכים הוכרח אברהם אבינו ע"ה לתת להם מים לרחוץ טרם הכנסם בביתו כדי שלא יכנסו בביתו עם האבק שהיו משתחוים לו לשום אלהות לא שהיו משתחוים לאבק שברגליהם ממש:

And wash your feet as you think they are Arabs, etc. The incident is noted in Bava Metziya 86b, perek haSocher es Poalim. And if he did not perform the wash, in the case of Lavan, who was not particular, why did he gave (Eliezer) water to wash (feet) (Bereshis 24:32)? And also Lot, who was not careful, because he offered spending night before washing (feet), why did he offer them to wash (Bereshis 19:2)? Rather, washing was a common custom for all wayfarers. But from the drasha of RZ"L in Bava Metziya 86b it is not so, because Abraham preceded washing (feet) to coming into (the tent) contrary to custom entering the tent and then washing (as Lot did).

It seems to me that the verse is not speaking simply (לאו דוקא) of the dust of the (travelers) feet. Rather, to all kinds of "dust" (i.e. materiality) the bow. And here it chose to speak of the dust of their feet because it is the way of travelers to have dust on their feet. Thus [Lot] was not particular about it when bringing [guests] into the house because he only focused on those who bow to stars themselves. Because anyone who learns wonders how is it possible for a human to bow to dust on one's feet, which is less than material amount? I would like to give reason to it. The ancient philosophers, such as the sect of Epicurus and his helpers, believed that all things that exist are composed of the individual particles that are the dust; and that by joining them one can bring to existence all things; and by separating them one can destroy all things; and that there is no force other than them, only these particles are god himself. Since the dust is always at the feet of wayfarers, Abraham our father was forced to give them water to bathe before entering his tent so that they would not enter his house with the dust that they would bow down as deification of materiality, not that they bowed down to the dust itself on their very feet:

The teachings of Epicurus are pretty much the foundation of the modern atheism. R. Mizrachi states that one cannot view these teachings other than avoda zara.

questions.title_en: Should buying an Etrog from Israel take precedence over Chutz laarerz?
questions.question: Is there an Inyan or Halacha to buy an etrog from Eretz Yisrael? Is there a מעלה of purchasing etrogim from Israel over other countries? Does it make a difference if the person asking this question is located inside or outside the land of Israel?

answers.text:
Yes.

The Aruch HaShulchan (after establishing that the Israeli esrogim were without concern of murkav whereas the Corfu esrogim were) concludes:

ולכן כל איש מישראל אשר נגע יראת ד' בלבו – לא יקח רק אתרוגי ארץ ישראל

Therefore, any Jew whose fear of God affects his heart shall take only of Israeli esrogim.

He then adds:

ואיך לא נבוש ולא נכלם בדבר מצוה שנוכל לקיימה מפרי ארצנו הקדושה, ליטול דווקא מארץ העמים? אוי לה לאותה בושה, אוי לה לאותה כלימה! ועל זה נאמר: וימאסו בארץ חמדה.

And how can one not be ashamed and humiliated — regarding a mitzva which he is able to perform through fruit of our holy land — to intentionally take from other lands? Woe for such a shame! Woe for such a humiliation! Regarding this it states "And they despised the cherished land."

(He lived in Lithuania and was not limiting his rulings to those living in Israel.)

It appears to be a machlokes depending on whether we have such a mesorah and the quality of that mesorah.

Halachipedia:

Many say that the etrogim from Eretz Yisrael have a good mesorah. Avnei Nezer CM 415 the Etrogim from Eretz Yisrael are the best because there were religious Jews living there the entire time of the exile, but because they’re difficult to get, we use Korfu. Taharat Haetrogim p. 298 cites this.

However, some claim that the etrogim from Eretz Yisrael have no mesora since religious Jews didn’t live there for many years before and after the Ramban (Taharat Haetrogim p. 299 quoting Sod Yesharim p. 356, Horat Heter p. 5. He also cites a testimony from R’ Yakov of Karaz that the minhag Yerushalayim was to use Korfu etrogim.).

However, others uphold the mesora of the etrogim from Israel. (Taharat Haetrogim p. 300 quoting Rav Meir Auerbach author of Imrei Binah (Nefesh Chaya OC 4). He also cites Rav Chaim Nissim Abulafia supporting those etrogim.).

questions.title_en: How does Devarim 28:68 jive with the opinion that positive public prophecies are never reversed?
questions.question:
Midrash Tanchuma (cited in Rashi to Yirmiyahu 28:7) and Rambam (hakdamah to peirush hamishnah) are of the opinion that only negative public and positive private prophecies can become undone with the betterment/deterioration of behavior respectively, but positive public prophecies can never be revoked, even if bad behavior develops.

Others argue (e.g. Abarbanel to Yirmiyahu ad loc and ibn Kaspi to Devarim 18:21) and say that even public positive prophecies can be voided with the development of bad behavior.

Devarim 28:68 reads:

וֶהֱשִׁיבְךָ יְהֹוָה מִצְרַיִם בׇּאֳנִיּוֹת בַּדֶּרֶךְ אֲשֶׁר אָמַרְתִּי לְךָ לֹא תֹסִיף עוֹד לִרְאֹתָהּ וְהִתְמַכַּרְתֶּם שָׁם לְאֹיְבֶיךָ לַעֲבָדִים וְלִשְׁפָחוֹת וְאֵין קֹנֶה.

Hashem will bring you into Egypt again with ships, by the way of which I said to you, "You shall see it no more again", and there you shall sell yourselves to your enemies for bondservants and for bondmaids, and no man shall buy you.

which refers to Shemos 14:13:

וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֶל הָעָם אַל תִּירָאוּ הִתְיַצְּבוּ וּרְאוּ אֶת יְשׁוּעַת יְהֹוָה אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה לָכֶם הַיּוֹם כִּי אֲשֶׁר רְאִיתֶם אֶת מִצְרַיִם הַיּוֹם לֹא תֹסִפוּ לִרְאֹתָם עוֹד עַד עוֹלָם.

Moshe said to the people, "Do not be afraid. Station yourselves and see Hashem's salvation that He will do for you today, for as you have seen Egypt today, you shall not see them ever again.

The Torah seems to be explicitly saying that the positive public prophecy will be reversed with the advent of deleterious behavior.

How would the first opinion account for it?

(Oddly, Abarbanel himself, to the Devarim verse, proffers a difficult suggestion in defense of the other opinion, I'm looking for something more straightforward)

answers.text: Perhaps the verse in Shemos is a command, not a prophecy. Not "I promise that you will never go back there again," but "I command you not to return there again." Alternatively, we could read it as referring to the people. "Today you have seen these people, but you will never see them again--for they will sink to the bottom of the sea."

questions.title_en: "It would have been better if they had not been born" - why?
questions.question:
I have seen the phrase "it would have been better if they had not been born" in regards to lots of sins.

Here is a sample.

I notice that this phrase can often be used in isolation, without any explanation. This guides me towards curiosity.

  • What are the origins of this phrase
  • Does it have a specific meaning or is it context based?
  • Why is it used so often without explaining itself. Ok, it would have been better to not have been born, but why? What was it like before and why is it now worse? In what way?
  • Why are we, against our will, put into a situation that could (so easily) end us up in a worse position than had we never been put into that situation? p.s. Why does it seem most of the time, it seems to be a phrase used when there are two outcomes, it is the failure state: a man should do x and he will be rewarded y, but if not it would have been better had he not been born
  • Is there any good news for the (seemingly many) unsuccessful ones, who "should never have been born"?

So, this question is regarding the phrase ונוח להם שלא נבראו and equivalent, & it seeks an answer that is able to deal with explaining it as properly and fully as possible. I suspect there probably is some source out there somewhere that tries to do so, but will accept whatever I can get that helps with the above questions regarding this specific phrase.

answers.text:
תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן שְׁתֵּי שָׁנִים וּמֶחֱצָה נֶחְלְקוּ בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וּבֵית הִלֵּל הַלָּלוּ אוֹמְרִים נוֹחַ לוֹ לְאָדָם שֶׁלֹּא נִבְרָא יוֹתֵר מִשֶּׁנִּבְרָא וְהַלָּלוּ אוֹמְרִים נוֹחַ לוֹ לְאָדָם שֶׁנִּבְרָא יוֹתֵר מִשֶּׁלֹּא נִבְרָא נִמְנוּ וְגָמְרוּ נוֹחַ לוֹ לְאָדָם שֶׁלֹּא נִבְרָא יוֹתֵר מִשֶּׁנִּבְרָא עַכְשָׁו שֶׁנִּבְרָא יְפַשְׁפֵּשׁ בְּמַעֲשָׂיו וְאָמְרִי לַהּ יְמַשְׁמֵשׁ בְּמַעֲשָׂיו ערובין יג ע"ב

The Rabbis taught: For two and a half years, Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel debated. One said that it would have been better (or maybe easier) for a man not to have been created, and the other said that it was better that he was created. They concluded that it would be better that he were not created, but now that he is created, he should examine his deeds; and some say, he should feel his deeds. Eruvin 13b

It seems to me that one of these schools of thought held that being given the opportunity to cling to Hashem is "worth it," even for someone that fell away from Him, while the other held that for someone that fell away from Him, the theoretical (but unutilized) opportunity to cling to Him has basically expired worthless. They concluded that the second approach was more correct, but noted that this only applies once a man is dead. While he is still alive, he can improve his deeds with mussar and cheshbon hanefesh, and he should do so.

As for the sources that apply the phrase "נח לו שלא נברא" to people that commit various sins, I think that they are pointing out that such people are indeed throwing away the opportunity of life, and we can apply to them the final decision that he would have been better off had he never been created

The good news for such people is that so long as they're alive, they can turn things around. And even after they're dead, it is possible that some merit will be found for them. For example, perhaps their children or grandchildren will do better, and this will redound to their benefit.

I note that the phrase used is frequently:

רָאוּי לוֹ כְּאִלּוּ לֹא בָּא לָעוֹלָם -- It would have been better FOR HIM if he had never come into the world.

I see the key word as "for him", not necessarily for the world -- meaning: To spare him pain. (E.g., in Chagigah 2:1)

questions.title_en: Alzheimer's and Dementia and counting for a minyan
questions.question:
I have tried to find any discussion or responsa on whether someone with dementia or alzheimer's would count for a minyan.

The obvious question is, are they with it enough to know what is being said, respond to amen etc.

Maybe it's taken on a case by case basis, maybe not. Either way, what are the halachic principles to apply to this question?

answers.text: If the person still knows where they are and what they’re doing—even for a short time—they can usually be counted in a minyan. It mostly depends on how aware they are. If they understand they’re praying with others, that’s a good sign. But if they are very confused and don’t know what’s going on, then they might not be able to count. These things are different for each person. It’s a good idea to ask a rabbi to be sure. Everyone deserves respect, no matter what they’re going through.

questions.title_en: Egyptian priests as closet monotheists, and Joseph’s Pharaoh as a Canaanite?
questions.question:
An exceptionally rare 1936 book by Rev Dr Izak Goller, called First Chapter, includes the following:

A powerful shepherd king of Canaan had invaded and conquered Egypt, and one of his descendants ruled from the throne of the Pharaohs, much to the annoyance of the Egyptians and their exiled dynasty […Joseph’s] death was followed by a general uprising that deposed the foreign dynasty, reinstated the old line of Pharaohs and bred a natural hatred for us due to our friendship and kinship with the hated usurpers … Moses, brought up in Pharaoh’s palace, received a princely education which included a knowledge of the One God undisclosed to the masses, among whom the Egyptian priests – for their own political purposes – cultivated the most absurd forms of idolatry.

This passage contains two narratives I’ve not seen before:

  1. Joseph’s Pharaoh was a Canaanite invader and there was a revolution between his death and the enslavement of the Israelites.
  2. The Egyptian priesthood were closet monotheists.

Did Rev Dr Goller invent these glosses or do we find them in any traditional sources? Thanks!

questions.title_en: Can you sing religious songs in the restroom?
questions.question: Is it allowed to sing in the restroom? I understand some customs hold that you shouldn't speak in the restroom, but what if someone enjoyed singing in the shower? Also, what if someone sang religious songs in the shower? Would you need to replace any words?

answers.text:
According to the Yabia Omer:

Regarding a room that houses a bathtub or shower nowadays, one may not recite any words of holiness in it. One is permitted, however, to think words of Torah in it and may therefore listen to a Torah lecture or holy songs from the radio and the like there.

Note: Obviously, the aforementioned Halacha applies only to a room that houses a bathtub or shower alone; however, if there is a toilet in the room, one may not even think words of Torah there.

• According to Shulchan Aruch OC 85:2, one is allowed to speak (or sing, what's the difference?) secular matters in a bathroom.

  • According Shulchan Aruch HaRav there, one should ideally (and probably halachically) not hum any melodies from Jewish songs (religious) in the bathroom, even without lyrics.

questions.title_en: Is there any reason to suppose that "Reish Lakish" means something like "chief of the bandits"?
questions.question:
I feel like I've heard this many times over the years. In the last couple of days I've shopped the question around, and everyone seems to have heard the theory that because of his colorful past, Reish Lakish was so-called because it means "chief of the bandits."

It doesn't seem to make much sense. Jastrow doesn't list such a word, Lakish = bandit. It seems hard to reconcile with the frequently-used Shimon Ben Lakish, unless that Ben is taken to mean something like the Ben of Ben Torah. And it would seem rather strange to call him forever by reference to his former bad character which he so greatly improved. To me it seems much more natural to assume that Reish is a contraction of Rav Shimon, used just because there were a lot of Shimons to be distinguished.

Anyhow, is there any source or good reason to the view that Reish Lakish means something like "chief of the bandits"?

answers.text:
R’ Yochanan (Bava Metzia 84a) refers to Reish Lakish as “Bar Lekisha”. The added alef seems to indicate that “Lakish” is more than just a name.

Lekisha translates as “the late one”. (See Targum Onkelos, Bereishis 30:42; Vayikra Rabbah 30:3.) This is one of the reasons the late rain is called מלקוש. Perhaps the name “Reish Lakish” alludes to his belated devotion to Torah study, dubbing him “the Latecomer” — and indeed, “the Head of the Latecomers”.

In reference to the name Reish Lakish, R. Reuven Margalit לחקר שמות וכינויים בתלמוד on page 6 points out midrash Bereshis Rabba 73:10, which ends with words:

רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ, רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר בַּכִּירַיָּא דְלָבָן, רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר לַקִּישַׁיָא דְלָבָן.

Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Those born earlier were Laban’s. Reish Lakish said: Those born later (lakishaya) were Laban’s.

The name signifies he was born later to his parents.

Alternatively, it seems that the nickname Reish Lakish of R. Shimon ben Lakish is a play on words. Lakish was the name of R. Shimon's father, and it means "the late one" as explained Yø-c Ro. However, for R. Shimon the nickname was used as a hint ריש מלקה איש - Reish Malkeh Ish - Chief hitter of men (Thank you Harel13!), as in Mishna Makkos 3:3 " לוֹקֶה אַרְבָּעִים " - flogged with forty lashes.

We can infer the etymology as follows. In the final conflict with R. Yochanan in Bava Metzia 84a R. Shimon b. Lakish says to R. Yochanah:

אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וּמַאי אַהֲנֵית לִי? הָתָם ״רַבִּי״ קָרוּ לִי, הָכָא ״רַבִּי״ קָרוּ לִי!

Reish Lakish said to Rabbi Yoḥanan: What benefit did you provide me by bringing me close to Torah? There, (among the bandits), they called me: Rabbi (literally Leader/Great Man), and here (among Torah scholars), too, they call me: Rabbi.

The description of what R. Shimon did before he became a rabbi is given in Gittin 47a also here

The Gemara recounts a related incident: Reish Lakish sold himself to gladiators. He took a bag and a round stone inside of it with him. He said: There is a tradition that on the final day of a captive’s life, before his captors kill him, they do for him anything that he requests of them, so that he would forgive them for the spilling of his blood. On the final day before they were set to kill him they said to him: What is amenable to you? He said to them: I want to tie you up and have you sit, and I will אֶמְחְיֵהּ/strike each one of you one and a half times. He tied them up and had each one of them sit. When he struck each of them with one strike with the stone in the bag, the one whom he struck died, because Reish Lakish was of great strength. Reish Lakish gritted his teeth in anger, and said to the one whom he killed, in order to prevent the others from realizing what was happening: Are you laughing at me? You still have half of a strike remaining with me, as I struck you only once. He killed them all, and Reish Lakish escaped his captors.

The Aramaic word מחי is the same as Hebrew מכה and מלקה is used in the context of מכות.

questions.question:
What is the proper nikkud of the feminine הפעיל in the present tense, + אותו? (E.g. מַחֲזִירָה + אוֺתוֺ.) I’ve seen it vowelized variously as ,מַחֲזִירְתּוֺ, מַחֲזִירַתּוּ and מַחֲזִירָתוֺ. (I’ve noticed the Kehati Mishnayos vowelizes pi’el in the present tense as מְשַׁמְרַתּוּ, although I had assumed this was an error.)

Does anyone know of any examples in Tanach where this form appears?

answers.text:
All of them are okay. The difference between cases 2 and 3 is probably if the word is in pause, if it's in pause then the shva probably turns into a qamets. The 1st case is also okay, it is just that the long form מַחֲזִירַתְהוּ, when the suffix gets swallowed up in the תּ it becomes מַחֲזִירַתּוּ, hence the dagesh for compensation.

It works the same way like in past verbs, the form זכרה becomes the form זְכָרַתְהוּ with a suffix (she remembered him) and then to זְכָרַתּוּ when the ה gets swallowed up in the תּ. The same happens to זְכָרַתְהָ (she remembered her), this always becomes זְכָרַתָּה, and always without mappik.

I don't think I could find sources for the present tense because even the past tense is hard to find, but they should both work the way way.

ישעיהו 59:16 זְכָרַתְהוּ

רות 4:15 זְכָרַתּוּ

ישעיהו 34:17 זְכָרַתָּה

questions.title_en: Do animals go extinct
questions.question:
The Chinuch, on the mitzva of shiluach hakein says the following:

מִשָּׁרְשֵׁי הַמִּצְוָה. לָתֵת אֶל לִבֵּנוּ שֶׁהַשְׁגָּחַת הָאֵל בָּרוּךְ הוּא עַל בְּרִיּוֹתָיו בְּמִין הָאָדָם בִּפְרָט, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (איוב לד, כא) כִּי עֵינָיו עַל כָּל דַּרְכֵי אִישׁ וְגוֹ' וּבִשְׁאָר מִינֵי בַּעֲלֵי חַיִּים בַּמִּינִים דֶּרֶךְ כְּלָל, כְּלוֹמַר שֶׁחֶפְצוֹ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּקִיּוּם הַמִּין, וְעַל כֵּן לֹא יִכְלֶה לְעוֹלָם מִין מִכָּל מִינֵי הַנִּבְרָאִים, כִּי בְּהַשְׁגָּחַת הַחַי וְקַיָּם לָעַד בָּרוּךְ הוּא עַל הַדָּבָר יִמָּצֵא בּוֹ הַקִּיּוּם. וּבְהַנִּיחַ הָאָדָם דַּעְתּוֹ עַל זֶה יָבִין דַּרְכֵי הַשֵּׁם, וְיִרְאֶה כִּי הַמְשָׁכַת קִיּוּם הַמִּינִין בָּעוֹלָם שֶׁלֹּא כָּלָה וְאָבַד אֶחָד מִכֻּלָּם, מִבֵּיצֵי כִּנִּים וְעַד קַרְנֵי רְאֵמִים מִיּוֹם שֶׁנִּבְרְאוּ, הַכֹּל בְּמַאֲמָרוֹ וְחֶפְצוֹ עַל זֶה.

It is from the roots of this commandment [that it is] to put into our hearts that the providence of God, may He be blessed, is upon all of His creatures — with the human species individually, as it is written (Job 34:21), “For His eyes are upon a man’s ways, etc.”; and upon the other species of animals generally, meaning to say that His desire, may He be blessed, is towards the existence of the [particular] species. And therefore, no species will ever become extinct from all of the species of creatures, as it is due to the providence of the Living and Existing forever, may He be blessed, that their existence is found.

Is this statement, that no species will ever become extinct, meant to be taken literally? Also, is this thought found in other sources?

answers.text:
Supposing that the Chinuch means exactly what it sounds like. If so, he's wrong. Empirically, we see that many species have become extinct. And therefore, his interpretation, moving as it is, is not correct.

This is not a problem for us. We're not committed to the idea that no Rishon could ever err. Rishonim made mistakes, and Amoraim made mistakes...even Moshe Rabbenu and the Avos and Imahos made a few mistakes.

Hashem is free of all error. Human beings, however great, err.

questions.title_en: Where does it say that Abraham rescues all Neshamos from gehinom?
questions.question: I heard from a sephardic guy that Abraham rescues all Neshamos from gehinom. There is a caveat that he doesn't help those who sleep with a gentile woman. Does anyone know the source?

answers.text:
The source is in Gemara (Eruvin 19a):

״עוֹבְרֵי בְּעֵמֶק הַבָּכָא״, הָהוּא דִּמְחַיְּיבִי הָהִיא שַׁעְתָּא בְּגֵיהִנָּם, וְאָתֵי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ וּמַסֵּיק לְהוּ וּמְקַבֵּל לְהוּ. בַּר מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁבָּא עַל הַגּוֹיָה, דְּמָשְׁכָה עׇרְלָתוֹ וְלָא מְבַשְׁקַר לֵיהּ.

Those who are liable at that time for punishment in Gehenna, but our father Abraham comes and raises them up and receives them. He does not leave the circumcised behind and allow them to enter Gehenna, except for a Jew who had relations with a gentile woman, in punishment for which his foreskin is drawn, and our father Abraham does not recognize him as one of his descendants. (Sefaria translation)

questions.title_en: Inserting other mitzvot between loan-related commandments
questions.question: In Berakhot 21b we learn that even those, who don't interpret the juxtaposition of different verses in the first four books of the Torah, they do so in the Book of Deuteronomy, because – as Ritva points out there among others – in Devarim Moses reiterated all the commandments he had heard from Hashem, so he consciously chose a logic order, which is not necessarily so in the previous books. Therefore, I found it unusual when I was reading Ki Teitzei that between two loan-related prohibitions (taking a millstone as a pledge and entering the house of a debtor) the prohibition of kidnapping and a reminder of tzaraat are interjected. I haven't seen Rashi commenting on this issue despite having done so a few verses earlier. Have you found any commentators discussing this seemingly strange insertion?

answers.text:
The Even Ezra gives an explanation. He quotes others that say because of this question, that the first passuk refers to husband and wife and not a millstone. He then argues and explains differently:

כי נפש הוא חובל – כי בו מחית נפשות, והסומכים על הסמך הפרשיות איננה טענה, כי כל מצו' עומדת בפני עצמה והסמיכות כדרך דרש. וזאת הפרש' דבקה, כי הזכיר שלא יגזול ענבים לתת אל כליו וחרמש בקמה, ולקחת אשה והיתה לו גם לאחר ויצא מרשותו, והלוקח אשה שישמח בה לא יהיה עשוק שיצא בצבא. וחביל' הרחים עושק וגם גונב נפש, וכן נגע הצרעת שלא ישמרו משפטיה תזיק הקרובים, וכן לא תעשוק העני בעבוטו והשכיר, והבנים הקטנים שלא ימותו בעון אביהם, והטיית משפט גר יתום וחבול בגד אלמנה, ושכחה בשדה כי היא לעני, וכן לא תעולל וכן פן יוסיף ונקלה, וחסימת השור עשק כי יגע ולא יאכל, והממאן ליבם כדמות עשק, והמחזקת במבושים עושקת, אבן ואבן איפה ואיפה עשק ממש, גם עמלק עשק לישראל:‏

For he taketh a man's life to pledge – For life is sustained by these instruments. Those who rely on the juxtaposition of the sections have no argument, (That our verse speaks metaphorically of sexual intercourse.) for each commandment stands by itself. (The commandments are not necessarily tied together. Each commandment is an independent unit.) The explanation of their juxtapositions is midrashic. (It therefore cannot be used as a reason to interpret a law metaphorically when the plain meaning of the text is acceptable.) This section (The law regarding taking a mill to pledge.) is connected to the previous ones in the following way: (That is, if we want to connect this section midrashically to what comes before, we can so in the following manner.) the Torah mentions that one is not to steal grapes by putting them in his pots (Deut. 23:25), or to lift up a sickle upon his neighbor’s grain (Deut. 23:26); or to take a woman after she has been his and then left his house and married another (v. 1). It also states that one has to cheer the woman whom he marries (v. 5); he is not to be oppressed by going into the army (Ibid.). The taking of a millstone in pledge is a form of oppression. (Hence the positioning of our law.) So too is kidnapping a person. Similarly the plague of leprosy, for if he does not observe its laws then the plague will injure those in proximity to it. (By infecting them.) Scripture similarly states, do not oppress a poor person by taking a pledge from him (v. 10). It similarly states do not oppress a hired person (v. 14) and small children should not be put to death for the sins of the fathers (v. 16). It likewise warns against perverting the justice due a stranger or the fatherless (v. 17). It prohibits the taking of a widow’s garment as a pledge (v. 17). It prohibits one from retrieving a sheaf which was forgotten in the field, for it belongs to the poor (v. 19). Similarly Thou shalt not glean (v. 21). Likewise lest if he should exceed…Then thy brother should be dishonored (Deut. 25:3). (Deut. 25:3 prohibits the infliction of more that 40 stripes to one being punished by lashes. Exceeding this number of stripes is a form of oppression.) The muzzling of an ox (v. 4) is an act of oppression, for the animal toils but cannot eat of its toil. Similarly, refusing to perform levirate marriage (Deut. 25:5-10) is a form of oppression. The woman who grabs a man’s testicles (Deut. 25:11) commits an act of oppression. Employing diverse weights and diverse measures (Deut. 25:13,14) is oppression in its purest form. Furthermore, Amalek oppressed Israel (Deut. 25:17-19). (Thus the laws in Deut. 23:25-25:19 are thematically related. Hence the law prohibiting the taking of a mill was included in this section.) (Sefaria)

questions.title_en: Did the Arizal's daughter marry the son of R' Yosef Karo?
questions.question:
Is there any source [historical, academic, mystical] that the Arizal's daughter married the son of R' Yosef Karo, author of Shulchan Aruch?

I see this mentioned in this article (unsourced), and noticed a similar claim on this forum (citing a story about the shidduch to 'Shivchei Ari' - I couldn't find this in a OCR search of Shivchei Ari).

answers.text:
The source for this legend is toward the end of Shivhei HaAri, by R. Shlomo Shlomil Ben Chaim. There, R. Shlomil writes the following story:

ואני הצעיר שלמה מעיד שדברתי עם אלמנותו של רי"ק ז"ל וסיפרה לי שמהררי"ק היה לו בן נחמד ושידך אותו עם בתו של האריז״ל והלך מהררי״ק עם בנו לסעודת אירוסין לביתו של האריז״ל כיון שחזר לביתו אמר מהררי״ק לאשתו אשתי אשתי מה אומר לך או מה אספר מהרזים ומהטעמי התורה והמצוה מה ידיעה הרווחתי עתה בזה הסעודה מפי הקדוש של ר׳ יצחק אשכנזי היכן הוא כח ביד שום מלאך לידע מה שיודע הוא אין זה כי אם נשמה אחת מהנביאים הראשונים שאפילו תנא אחר אינו יכול לומר מה שאמר הוא אבל אני מפחד עליו בעו״ה מאור שזה הדור הגרוע לא יכול לסבול רוב קדושתו ויוקח ויאבד מהם בקוצר שנים בעונות וכן היה

And I, the young Shlomo, testify that I spoke with Rav Yosef Karo's widow and she told me that Rav Karo had a fine son and matched him with the daughter of the Arizal. And it went, that after Rav Karo went with his son to the engagement meal at the Arizal's house he returned to his home and Rav Karo said to his wife: "My wife, my wife, what can I say or tell you of the mysteries of the Torah and Mitzvot? How much knowledge have I now gained during this feast from the holy mouth of R. Yitzchak Ashkenazi [Luria]. He holds knowledge beyond what any angel knows, and there's no doubt he has the soul of one of the early prophets. Even a Tanna could not teach what he taught. But I am afraid for him. It is clear that this is the worst generation, which cannot tolerate his holiness, and he will be taken away and lost to them at an early age." And so it was.

Does this mean their children indeed married? It's hard to know. R. Shlomil came to Tzfat some 30 years after the Arizal died, and his book mixes verifiable historical information with many folkloric legends about the miracles and powers of the Arizal. So take it with a grain of salt.

That the Arizal and R. Yosef Karo knew each other is undisputed, as we have a teshuva from R. Karo, answering a question posed by the Arizal on the halakha of a business after a partner dies (cf. Avkat Rokhel #136).

In the book “Between Cross and Crescent” the author cites a midrash which apparently says: “God revealed himself in four languages: Hebrew, Latin, Arabic and Aramaic”

"Variantly: When the L-rd appeared to give Torah to Israel, He did so not with one language, but with four, viz.: "And the L-rd came from Sinai" - this is Hebrew, "And shone upon them from Seir" - this is Latin (lit. the language of Rome), "[He] appeared from Mount Paran" - this is Arabic, "And approached from Ribeboth-kodesh" - this is Aramaic."

questions.title_en: Chazan's repetitions for verses right after opening the Ark for the Torah
questions.question:
After opening Ark to get sefer Torah on Shabbos and Yom Tov in Ashkenazy custom many congregations sing verses:

כִּי מִצִּיּון תֵּצֵא תורָה. וּדְבַר ה' מִירוּשָׁלָיִם: בָּרוּךְ שֶׁנָּתַן תּורָה לְעַמּו יִשרָאֵל בִּקְדֻשָּׁתו:

What is a reason for a double repetition of phrases: כִּי מִצִּיּון תֵּצֵא תורָה and בָּרוּךְ שֶׁנָּתַן תּורָה, i.e. what was the intention of the composer of the tune?

The fact that the word תּורָה is repeated as תּורָה-תּורָה when singing בָּרוּךְ שֶׁנָּתַן sounds as if it refers to both written and oral Torah in opposition to Reform not accepting the oral Torah. Why would some chazanim avoid making these repetitions?

answers.text:
There are many melodies written for the paragraph beginning "Vay'hi Binsoa", but by far the most common one is by Salomon Sulzer. Interestingly, his setting is in his Yom Tov section of his book; he has a different Shabbat setting that no one uses.

He does indeed repeat the phrase כִּי מִצִּיּון תֵּצֵא תורָה twice. It's hard to infer exactly what his intent was here, but suffice to say it is a classic example of a sequence ascending by a tone, which is a typical compositional technique, and is pleasing to the ear as we recognise what we've already heard.

But Sulzer's melody stops at "Mirushalayim" and does not have anything written for בָּרוּךְ שֶׁנָּתַן תּורָה. So what you hear in North American congregations where the same melody from כִּי מִצִּיּון is applied to this verse is a later adaptation that Sulzer never wrote. I have heard some Rabbis and Chazzanim are opposed to this repetition of the word Torah for theological reasons, but know that it was never part of the original composition.

Outside of North America, it is more common to attach on a different, rising ending for בָּרוּךְ שֶׁנָּתַן תּורָה which actually comes from an earlier traditional melody. You can hear that full composition here: https://youtu.be/mGm22rCCnIA?si=8gghQvz_LrNhVZwM

questions.title_en: What does Bereshit Rabbah mean when it says the Scriptures spoke untruths?
questions.question: As far as I can tell Bereshit Rabbah 48:18 says that G-d actually repeated everything Sarah said to Abraham including that he was old, but the Torah falsely says that G-d only told Abraham that Sarah said that she was old in order to avoid strife between Abraham and Sarah. How does this fit with the belief that the scriptures are inerrant, especially since this passage seems to make perfect sense with its plain meaning?

answers.text:
You misunderstand the text. Let's take a look.

“The Lord said to Abraham: Why is it that Sarah laughed, saying: Shall I indeed bear a child, and I have grown old?” (Genesis 18:13). “The Lord said to Abraham: Why is it that Sarah laughed, saying: [Shall I indeed bear a child, and I have grown old?]” – bar Kappara said: Peace [between spouses] is a great thing, as even Scripture spoke untruths in order to establish peace between Abraham and Sarah. “Sarah laughed to herself, saying: After my languishing, shall I have youth, and my husband is old?” But He did not say this to Abraham, but rather, “Why is it that Sarah laughed, saying: Shall I indeed bear a child, and I have grown old?” The verse does not say as Sarah said: “My husband is old,” but rather, “I have grown old.”

The Medrash notes that Hashem deliberately misreported Sarah's comments to Avraham. Whereas she had commented that her husband, Avraham, was old, Hashem told Avraham that she had said that she herself was old. This was not an error on His part, nor an error on the part of the Torah as to what He said. He said this, and He said it intentionally. The purpose was to uphold marital peace between Avraham and Sarah, as Avraham might feel offended if he heard that his wife regarded him as elderly.

Again, when Sarah heard that she would yet have a child, she said "How can this be? My husband is too old."

When Hashem discussed this with Avraham, He said that Sarah had said "How can this be? I am too old."

Chazal note the discrepancy, and explain that Hashem is here teaching us that it is correct behavior to tell "white lies" in order to maintain peace between people, particularly between married couples.

questions.title_en: Source of Chofetz Chaim’s Statement on Every Nation Having Translated Bibles and Believing in the Revelation at Mount Sina
questions.question:
In the Sefer Taharas Yisroel (chapter 1), the Chofetz Chaim claims that all nations (in his time) believed in the revelation at Mount Sinai recorded in the Bible and had copies of the Bible in their own language.

The phrase "all nations on earth from one end to the other" suggests that he was referring to every nation without exception. Furthermore, the chapter's context suggests that he refers to every nation. He aims to highlight the utter foolishness of those who reject the Torah, as all nations accept its story. His argument loses much of its force if the Bible is acknowledged solely by Christianity and Islam rather than universally.

What is the source of this?

I find it hard to believe that Hindus, Buddhists, and all the Indigenous peoples of Africa, South America, and Australia had copies of the Bible, let alone believe it.

He does cite a verse in Parshas Nitzavim which states that all nations will acknowledge Israel's suffering as a consequence of abandoning their covenant with God. However, employing this as evidence to discredit Torah skeptics is circular reasoning. It claims they are foolish for disputing something supposedly recognized by all nations, yet the sole claim to its universal acknowledgment is the Torah itself.
